vignette:
He is 65, an African man who has spent most of his adult life working in retail, the kind of person who knows how to keep shelves straight, greet customers warmly, and notice when something is out of place before anyone else does. He is married, and when he speaks about his life before the disaster, he describes it in practical, modest terms: work, church, family meals, small routines that made the days feel reliable. He had never thought of himself as a fearful man. He saw himself as steady.

The event that changed that began with rain that did not stop.

At first, he treated it the way many people in his community did, as an inconvenience that would pass. He moved a few things higher off the floor, checked on neighbors, and tried to reassure his wife. But the water kept rising. The roads disappeared first, then the yard, then the first step of the house. He remembers the strange disbelief of watching familiar things become dangerous. He can still picture household items floating where they did not belong, hear people shouting over the sound of water and wind, feel the panicked urgency in his chest as he and his wife tried to gather documents, clothes, medicines, anything they could carry.

What stays with him most is not a single dramatic image but a series of moments that now return to him without warning: the cold water pushing against his legs, the smell of mud and fuel, his wife’s face when the lights went out, the helplessness of leaving behind things he had worked for over decades. They were evacuated with others from the neighborhood. In the shelter, surrounded by noise and confusion, he could not settle. He stayed alert through the night, watching doors, tracking sounds, feeling responsible for noticing danger before it reached them. Even after they were physically safe, his body did not seem to understand that the emergency had ended.

In the months afterward, he told himself he should be grateful. They survived. Some people lost more. He returned to work in retail as soon as he could, partly because the income was necessary and partly because he hoped normal routine would restore him. Instead, he finds that ordinary stress now overwhelms him. When there is heavy rain, even a regular storm, he feels his chest tighten before he is fully aware of what is happening. At work, if he hears rushing water from a broken pipe, a bucket spilling, or the metallic crash of stock falling, his whole body jerks. He becomes drenched in sweat and has to pretend he is only tired or overheated.

He does not talk much about the disaster unless pressed. His wife notices that he turns off the television when there is news footage of flooding, storms, or displaced families. He avoids roads near the river and becomes irritated if she asks why they cannot visit certain parts of town. He used to enjoy sitting outside in the evenings, but now he prefers to remain indoors where he can see exits and monitor the weather forecast. He checks it repeatedly, several times a day, as if vigilance might prevent another catastrophe. If rain is predicted, he grows restless and short-tempered. He moves items off the floor, charges phones, rechecks important papers, and barely sleeps.

Sleep has become one of the hardest parts. He wakes suddenly, heart pounding, sometimes from dreams in which the house is filling with water and he cannot find his wife. At other times he cannot remember the dream, only the terror that lingers in his body. His wife tells him that he thrashes in bed and calls out. In the morning he feels ashamed and exhausted. He has begun taking naps in a chair rather than lying down, saying he rests better that way, though he knows he is never deeply asleep.

He also notices changes in himself that trouble him more quietly. He feels older since the flood, not simply in years but in spirit. At work he can still do what is required, but it takes more effort to concentrate. If a customer raises their voice or a delivery arrives unexpectedly, he loses track of what he is doing. He sometimes stares at water bottles lined on a shelf and is suddenly back in that house, trying to decide what can be saved. On those days he feels far away from everyone. He smiles because that is what the job requires, but he feels detached, as though part of him is still standing in floodwater.

His wife says he is present but not fully with her. He knows what she means. He loves her, but he has become withdrawn, less affectionate, more easily angered. He feels guilty about this and guilty, too, that he survived when others did not recover as he did materially. He tells himself to be strong, to stop dwelling on the past, yet the past keeps arriving in his body before his mind can push it away. Now, even years later, each storm season feels to him not like a memory but like a warning, as though the disaster is still waiting just outside the door.
